question_text: The graph of $y = f'(x)$ is shown alongside.

subparts.stem: For what values of $x$ is $f(x)$ increasing?

mark_breakdown.desc: Read interval from given graph as $x \le x_1$

subparts.solution: $f(x)$ is increasing when $f'(x) \ge 0$. From the graph of $f'$, this occurs for $x \le x_1$.

ai_explanation.concept_rule: A function is increasing where the graph of its derivative lies above or on the $x$-axis.
step_by_step: Inspect the provided graph of $y = f'(x)$.
Locate where $y \ge 0$, which is to the left of $x_1$.
Conclude that $f(x)$ is increasing for $x \le x_1$.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Looking for where $f'(x)$ is sloping upward instead of where its values are positive.

subparts.stem: For what values of $x$ is $f(x)$ concave down?

mark_breakdown.desc: State that concavity down corresponds to $f'(x)$ decreasing
Read intervals from the graph: $x \le x_2$ and $x \ge x_3$

subparts.solution: $f(x)$ is concave down when $f'(x)$ is decreasing. From the graph, $f'(x)$ is decreasing for $x \le x_2$ and $x \ge x_3$.

ai_explanation.concept_rule: Concavity is determined by whether the derivative $f'(x)$ is increasing (concave up) or decreasing (concave down).
step_by_step: Identify local extrema of $f'(x)$: local minimum at $x_2$ and local maximum at $x_3$.
Determine intervals where $f'(x)$ has a negative slope (decreasing): to the left of $x_2$ and to the right of $x_3$.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Confusing intervals where $f'(x)$ is negative with intervals where $f'(x)$ is decreasing.

subparts.stem: Given that $y = f(x)$ passes through the origin, sketch the graph of $y = f(x)$.
subparts.final_answer: $Graph of $y = f(x)$ with local maximum at $x_1$, point of inflection at $x_2$, and stationary inflection point at $x_3$$

mark_breakdown.desc: Show maximum at $x_1$ and decreasing trend thereafter
Accurately show inflections at $x_2$ and stationary inflection at $x_3$

subparts.solution: The graph of $y = f(x)$ increases to a local maximum at $x = x_1$, then decreases. It changes concavity from downwards to upwards at $x = x_2$ (inflection point), and at $x = x_3$, it has a horizontal tangent ($f'(x_3) = 0$) where it changes concavity from upwards back to downwards, forming a stationary point of inflection.

ai_explanation.concept_rule: Translate features of $f'(x)$ to $f(x)$: zeros where sign changes give local extrema; tangent touching the axis gives stationary inflection points; extrema of $f'$ give inflection points.
step_by_step: $f'(x)$ crosses from positive to negative at $x_1 \implies$ local maximum at $x_1$.
$f'(x)$ has a minimum at $x_2 \implies$ inflection point at $x_2$ where concavity changes from down to up.
$f'(x)$ touches 0 at $x_3$ with a local maximum $\implies$ stationary inflection point at $x_3$ with concavity changing from up to down.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Drawing a local extremum at $x_3$ instead of a stationary point of inflection.

subparts.final_answer: $Graph of $y = f''(x)$ with $x$-intercepts at $x_2$ and $x_3$, positive on $(x_2, x_3)$ and negative elsewhere$

mark_breakdown.desc: Identify $x$-intercepts of $f''(x)$ at turning points of $f'(x)$ ($x_2$ and $x_3$)
Sketch curve crossing $x$-axis at $x_2$ and $x_3$, with a maximum between them

subparts.solution: The graph of $y = f''(x)$ represents the gradient of $f'(x)$. It is zero at the turning points of $f'(x)$, which are $x = x_2$ and $x = x_3$. It is negative for $x < x_2$, positive for $x_2 < x < x_3$, and negative for $x > x_3$. Thus, it is an inverted curve crossing the axis at $x_2$ and $x_3$.

ai_explanation.concept_rule: The second derivative is the slope of the first derivative: zeros occur at extrema of $f'$, positive where $f'$ is increasing, negative where $f'$ is decreasing.
step_by_step: Find where the slope of $f'(x)$ is zero: at the local min $x_2$ and local max $x_3$.
For $x < x_2$ and $x > x_3$, $f'(x)$ decreases, so $f''(x) < 0$.
Sketch an inverted curve with roots at $x_2$ and $x_3$.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Placing the $x$-intercepts of $f''(x)$ at $x_1$ instead of at the turning points $x_2$ and $x_3$.
